status: outcomes from KICD's text, word for word; skills, prerequisites and misconceptions proposed (authored offline, 13 Nov 2026), awaiting teacher review; depth pass 18 Nov 2026 (a skill for every testable outcome, two or more prerequisites and four misconceptions per skill, practical outcomes marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric, teaching pack in curriculum/agriculture/teaching/g6)

learning_experiences: watch video clips or observe photographs or make field excursions to observe types of soil erosion,
demonstrate how to control various types of soil erosion (gulley, rill, splash and sheet erosion),
discuss and make class presentations to appreciate the importance of controlling soil erosion to conserve soil in their environment.
key_inquiry_questions: How does erosion control conserve the environment?
sub_strands.core_competences: Critical thinking and problem solving: evaluation and decision making skills as learners explore appropriate ways of controlling soil erosion.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: proactively solving problems by taking appropriate measures to control soil erosion.
sub_strands.pcis: Environmental awareness as learners undertake control of soil erosion in the school environment.
sub_strands.links: Learners relate control of soil erosion to knowledge on conservation of natural resources learnt in Social Studies.

outcomes.text: describe types of soil erosion in the environment
control soil erosion in the environment
appreciate importance of conserving soil

skills.name: Name the types of soil erosion and what causes them
skills.mastery: The child names splash erosion (raindrops knock soil loose), sheet erosion (a thin layer is washed away evenly), rill erosion (small channels cut in the soil) and gully erosion (deep channels), and names causes (heavy rain, bare ground, cutting trees, overgrazing, ploughing up and down a slope). The child does not say a gully is a thin layer. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the type from its description
say which type is the most harmful
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 Agriculture and Nutrition introduced it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Grade 5 picked out bare and washed sites; Grade 6 names the kind of erosion seen there. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Raindrops and running water are forces that move soil. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.name: Pick the right way to control soil erosion on a slope
skills.mastery: The child names ways to control erosion (terraces and contour ploughing across the slope, planting trees, grass or cover crops, mulching, grass strips, closing a gully with stones and planting it), says each works by slowing the water or holding the soil, and does not plough up and down a slope or leave it bare. This is the knowledge half of outcome b; doing it is practical. The practical (controlling erosion on a school slope) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the control for a site
say which action makes erosion worse
find the false step in a learner's plan

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Mulching with plant remains, from Grade 5, is one way of controlling erosion. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.assessed_by: teacher marks the practical with the KICD rubric

misconceptions.error: Mixes up the names of the types of erosion.

example.question: Which erosion removes a thin layer of soil evenly?
example.correct_answer: Sheet erosion

misconceptions.cause: The child knows the words but not what each looks like.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Gully erosion" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw each type: sheet is a thin sheet, rill is a small channel, gully is a deep channel.
misconceptions.feedback: Sheet erosion removes a thin layer evenly. Gully erosion cuts deep channels.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says a gully is a thin layer or a small mark.

example.question: What is gully erosion?
example.wrong_answer: A thin layer of soil washed away evenly
example.correct_answer: Deep channels cut in the soil by running water

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks every kind of erosion is small.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A thin layer of soil washed away evenly" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a photo of a gully next to a rill.
misconceptions.feedback: A gully is a deep channel cut by running water. It is the most harmful kind.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Names a cause that does not cause erosion, or says erosion has no human cause.

example.question: Which action causes soil erosion?
example.correct_answer: Cutting down the trees on a slope

misconceptions.cause: The child does not link bare ground with washing away.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Planting grass on the slope" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pour water on bare soil and on soil with grass and compare.
misconceptions.feedback: Cutting trees and leaving the ground bare lets rain wash the soil away.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Ploughs up and down a slope.

example.question: How should a slope be ploughed?
example.correct_answer: Across the slope, along the contour

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks straight rows are best.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Up and down the slope" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pour water down furrows that go up and down and across.
misconceptions.feedback: Rows across the slope hold the water back. Rows up and down let it run away.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves the ground bare or cuts the cover.

example.question: Which action helps control erosion?
example.wrong_answer: Clearing all the plants from the slope
example.correct_answer: Planting grass and trees on the slope

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks a clean field is a good field.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Clearing all the plants from the slope" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare a bare slope and a grassed slope in rain.
misconceptions.feedback: Plants and mulch hold the soil. Bare ground washes away.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks letting animals graze freely protects the soil.

example.question: How does overgrazing affect the soil?
example.wrong_answer: It protects the soil with manure
example.correct_answer: It leaves the ground bare so it washes away

misconceptions.cause: The child links animals with manure only.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It protects the soil with manure" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Look at a heavily grazed patch and a fenced patch.
misconceptions.feedback: Overgrazing eats the cover and leaves the soil bare to wash away.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks splash erosion is caused by people splashing water, not by raindrops hitting bare soil.

example.question: What causes splash erosion?
example.correct_answer: Raindrops hitting bare soil and throwing it up

misconceptions.cause: The child takes the word "splash" from play.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "People splashing water about" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Drop water from a height on bare soil on white paper: look at the soil specks thrown up.
misconceptions.feedback: Raindrops hitting bare soil throw it up and loosen it. That is splash erosion.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a gully is controlled by filling it with rubbish and polythene.

example.question: How can a growing gully be controlled?
example.wrong_answer: Fill it with rubbish and polythene
example.correct_answer: Build checks of stones or sticks across it and plant grass

misconceptions.cause: The child sees a hole and thinks of filling it with anything.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Fill it with rubbish and polythene" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a gully with stone checks holding soil behind them.
misconceptions.feedback: Stone or stick checks across a gully slow the water and trap soil. Plant grass to hold it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: watch video clips or observe photographs or visit sites to observe sunken bed and shallow pits,
prepare seedbeds that conserve moisture (sunken seedbed and shallow pit),
utilise the sunken seedbed and shallow pits to appreciate the importance of soil moisture conservation in crop production.
key_inquiry_questions: How can we prepare a seedbed to conserve moisture?
sub_strands.core_competences: Critical thinking and problem solving: open mindedness and creativity as learners look for possibilities for conserving soil moisture.
sub_strands.values: Social justice: fairness and justice as learners share tasks and responsibilities in preparation of seedbeds.
sub_strands.pcis: Conservation of resources as learners conserve water through preparation of water conserving seedbeds.
sub_strands.links: Learners relate conservation of soil moisture to farming activities learnt in Social Studies.

outcomes.text: identify types of seedbeds that conserve soil moisture
prepare different types of seedbeds that conserve soil moisture
appreciate importance of conserving moisture in a seedbed to increase chances of plants growth

skills.name: Say which seedbeds keep soil moisture and how to keep a seedbed moist
skills.mastery: The child says a sunken bed (a bed dug below the ground level) holds water and suits a dry place, that a raised bed drains fast and suits a very wet place, that a flat bed lies between the two, and that mulch (dry grass or leaves on the bed) keeps the soil moist. Preparing a seedbed is practical. The practical (preparing a sunken seedbed and shallow pits) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the bed for a dry place
pick the bed for a wet place
find the false step in a learner's plan

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 Agriculture and Nutrition introduced it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Grade 5 named ways of conserving water in a garden; sunken beds are one. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Preparing a seedbed was learnt in Grade 4. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.assessed_by: teacher marks the practical with the KICD rubric

misconceptions.error: Says a raised bed is best in a dry place.

example.question: Which seedbed keeps moisture best in a dry place?
example.correct_answer: A sunken bed

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks higher means better.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A raised bed" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pour water on a raised and a sunken bed and watch which keeps it.
misconceptions.feedback: A sunken bed holds water in a dry place. A raised bed drains fast.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says a sunken bed is best in a very wet place.

example.question: Which seedbed suits a very wet place?
example.correct_answer: A raised bed

misconceptions.cause: The child does not think about waterlogging.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A sunken bed" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pour a lot of water on both beds.
misconceptions.feedback: A raised bed drains well in a very wet place. A sunken bed would flood.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves the seedbed uncovered after sowing.

example.question: What does mulch do on a seedbed?
example.correct_answer: It keeps the soil moist and cool

misconceptions.cause: The child does not see water leaving the bare soil.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing, it only looks tidy" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Cover one bed with dry grass and leave one bare in the sun.
misconceptions.feedback: Mulch shades the soil so less water evaporates.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks shallow pits are dug and planted with no manure.

example.question: What is put in a shallow planting pit before planting?
example.correct_answer: Manure or compost mixed with topsoil

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks the pit only catches water.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing, the pit is enough" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Grow two pits, one with manure; compare after a month.
misconceptions.feedback: Put manure in the pit with the topsoil. The pit holds water and the manure feeds the crop.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: search for information on physical deterrents search such as mesh fences, thorny fences, safe traps, innovative lights, innovative sounds, and deflectors,
select and establish a deterrent applicable in their local context,
discuss with a resource person the use of physical deterrents to acknowledge the importance of conserving wild animals in safeguarding crops and domestic animals.
key_inquiry_questions: How can wild animals be kept away from crops and domestic animals?
sub_strands.core_competences: Creativity and imagination: exploration skills as learners seek new ideas to establish physical deterrents against wild animals that destroy crops and domestic animals.
sub_strands.values: Patriotism: consciousness of social and moral duties to conserve wild animals and promote biodiversity.
sub_strands.pcis: Protection of biodiversity against extinction by deterring them without killing them.
sub_strands.links: Learners relate conservation of wild animals through use of deterrents to knowledge on importance of wildlife learnt in Social Studies.

outcomes.text: identify deterrents that can keep off wild animals from crop and domestic animals
establish deterrents to keep off wild animals from destroying crops and domestic animals
acknowledge the importance of deterrents in conserving wild animals

skills.name: Pick a safe deterrent for each wild animal that raids a farm
skills.mastery: The child picks a deterrent that keeps the animal away without killing it (a scarecrow or shiny strips for birds, a beehive fence, a chilli fence or a trench for elephants, a thorn or live fence, noise from a tin or a guard dog), says wild animals must be kept away and not killed, and does not pick poison or a snare. Setting a deterrent up is practical. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the deterrent for an animal
say why the animal is not killed
find the false step in a learner's plan

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 Agriculture and Nutrition introduced it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Grade 5 chose safe repelling methods; Grade 6 names physical deterrents. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.name: Say how a deterrent is put up and kept working
skills.mastery: Says how a chosen deterrent (mesh fence, thorny fence, light, noise maker or deflector) is put up: sited where the animals come in, built from local materials, checked and repaired, and moved or changed so animals do not get used to it; in the app the child picks the right step, order, tool or reason in new situations. The practical (establishing a deterrent in the local context) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: The child chooses the deterrent before putting it up. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Knowing where and when the animal raids tells where to put the deterrent. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.assessed_by: teacher marks the practical with the KICD rubric

misconceptions.error: Says wild animals that raid crops should be killed or poisoned.

example.question: What should a farmer do about elephants that raid his crops?
example.correct_answer: Use a beehive fence or chilli to keep them away

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks the only way to protect crops is to kill.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Set poison to kill them" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Discuss why wild animals are conserved and how deterrents work.
misconceptions.feedback: Wild animals are conserved. We keep them away from crops and do not kill them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Picks a deterrent that does not suit the animal.

example.question: Which deterrent keeps birds off the crops?
example.correct_answer: A scarecrow or shiny strips

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes the deterrents.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A beehive fence" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Match each animal to what it fears.
misconceptions.feedback: A scarecrow and shiny strips scare birds. A beehive fence keeps elephants away.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says a snare or trap is a deterrent.

example.question: Which is a safe deterrent?
example.wrong_answer: A snare set along the path
example.correct_answer: Noise from a tin or a guard dog

misconceptions.cause: The child does not tell a trap from a deterrent.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A snare set along the path" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: A deterrent keeps the animal away. A snare harms it.
misconceptions.feedback: A deterrent keeps animals away without hurting them. A snare traps and harms.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a deterrent must hurt the animal to work.

example.question: How does a deterrent protect crops?
example.wrong_answer: By hurting or killing the animal
example.correct_answer: By keeping it away without harming it

misconceptions.cause: The child links protection with punishment.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "By hurting or killing the animal" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask whether a bright light at night hurts a bush pig, and what it does.
misconceptions.feedback: A deterrent keeps animals away without harming them. It protects crops and wildlife.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves gaps at the bottom of a mesh fence.

example.question: Why must the bottom of a mesh fence touch or go into the ground?
example.correct_answer: Animals push or dig under any gap

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures animals jumping over, not crawling under.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It does not matter" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show tracks under a fence gap in a picture.
misconceptions.feedback: Close the gaps at the bottom. Many animals push or dig under a fence.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a deterrent put up once works for ever.

example.question: A solar light has kept porcupines away for a month. Now they are back. Why?
example.wrong_answer: The light is broken for ever
example.correct_answer: The animals got used to it; change or move it

misconceptions.cause: The child does not know animals learn that a thing is harmless.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The light is broken for ever" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare with the scarecrow from Grade 4: birds got used to it when it was not moved.
misconceptions.feedback: Animals get used to a deterrent that never changes. Move it or change it often.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a live thorny fence (such as kei apple or sisal) keeps animals out from the day it is planted.

example.question: A school plants a kei apple hedge to keep out goats and hares. When will it work?
example.wrong_answer: The same day it is planted
example.correct_answer: After it has grown thick, in a year or more; protect the crop meanwhile

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of the fence as finished once it is in the ground.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The same day it is planted" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show young hedge plants with wide gaps between them.
misconceptions.feedback: A live fence works only when it has grown thick. Use dry thorns or mesh until then.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts the deterrent in the middle of the farm instead of where the animals come in.

example.question: Where should a deflector or fence be put?
example.wrong_answer: In the middle of the garden
example.correct_answer: Along the path or edge where the animals come in

misconceptions.cause: The child puts it near the crop to guard.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "In the middle of the garden" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw the animal paths on a farm sketch and mark where they enter.
misconceptions.feedback: Put the deterrent where the animals enter, before they reach the crop.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: share experiences on routine practices in rearing of small domestic animals,
rear small domestic animal such as rabbits or guinea pigs to practise routine practices such as housing, feeding, watering, sanitation and parasite control.
make presentations to advocate the rearing of small domestic animals that are used for food.
key_inquiry_questions: How does rearing of animals contribute to food production?
sub_strands.core_competences: Self-efficacy: self-realization and confidence as learners rear small domestic animals such as rabbits for food production.
sub_strands.values: Integrity: fairness in allocation of resources and tasks in the project for rearing small domestic animals.
sub_strands.pcis: Animal welfare in the handling and caring for small domestic animals.
sub_strands.links: Learners relate rearing of small domestic animals to knowledge of farming as a socio-economic activity learnt in Social Studies.

outcomes.text: explain routine practices in rearing of small domestic animals
rear small domestic animals used as sources of food
embrace the rearing of small domestic animals used as sources of food

skills.name: Say the routine practices in rearing rabbits and chickens
skills.mastery: The child says daily jobs are feeding on proper feed, giving clean water, and checking each animal, that the house is cleaned and kept dry, that animals are vaccinated and dewormed as advised, that a sick animal is separated and the adult or animal health worker is told, and that records are kept. The child does not say any scraps will do or that water is optional. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say how often a job is done
say what a sick animal needs
find the false step in a learner's plan

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 Agriculture and Nutrition introduced it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Grade 5 related animals to their uses; Grade 6 rears small ones for food. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.name: Say how a rabbit hutch is set up and how the animals are fed, watered and kept healthy
skills.mastery: Says how small animals are reared: a raised, airy, dry hutch safe from predators, fed greens and dry feed daily, clean water always, droppings removed, parasites checked, sick animals separated; in the app the child picks the right step, order, tool or reason in new situations. The practical (rearing rabbits or guinea pigs at school) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: The routine practices are named before they are carried out. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Animals need food, water, air and shelter, the characteristics of living things. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.assessed_by: teacher marks the practical with the KICD rubric

misconceptions.error: Says water is optional or only when they look thirsty.

example.question: How often do rabbits and chickens need clean water?
example.correct_answer: Every day, fresh and clean

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks they get water from the food.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only when they look thirsty" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Check a trough left for a day.
misconceptions.feedback: Animals need clean water every day.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves the house dirty and wet.

example.question: How should the animal house be kept?
example.correct_answer: Clean and dry, with the droppings removed often

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks droppings do not matter.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Wet and left for weeks" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Discuss how dirt spreads disease.
misconceptions.feedback: A clean, dry house helps the animals stay healthy.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves a sick animal with the others and tells no one.

example.question: A chicken looks sick. What should you do?
example.wrong_answer: Leave it with the others and say nothing
example.correct_answer: Separate it and tell the teacher or the animal health worker

misconceptions.cause: The child does not think disease spreads.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Leave it with the others and say nothing" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Role play a sick chicken.
misconceptions.feedback: Separate a sick animal and tell an adult or health worker.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Lifts a rabbit by its ears.

example.question: How should a rabbit be lifted?
example.correct_answer: With one hand under the chest and the other supporting the rump

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen rabbits carried by the ears and thinks the long ears are handles.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "By the ears" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show the correct hold on a soft toy; ask where the rabbit's weight is.
misconceptions.feedback: Never lift a rabbit by its ears. Support its body under the chest and rump.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Builds the hutch on the bare ground.

example.question: Why is a rabbit hutch raised off the ground?
example.wrong_answer: It does not need to be
example.correct_answer: To keep it dry and away from rats, dogs and snakes

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures a hen house on the ground.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It does not need to be" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what happens to a hutch on the ground when it rains.
misconceptions.feedback: Raise the hutch so it stays dry and predators cannot reach the rabbits.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Feeds rabbits wet or wilted greens straight after rain.

example.question: What greens should rabbits be fed?
example.correct_answer: Fresh greens wilted slightly in the shade, not wet

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks wet leaves give the rabbit water too.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Wet or wilted leaves" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask the teacher about bloat and runny droppings from wet greens.
misconceptions.feedback: Give rabbits fresh, dry greens. Wet or mouldy feed upsets their stomachs.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts many rabbits in one small hutch to save space.

example.question: Why should a hutch not be overcrowded?
example.correct_answer: Crowded animals fight, get dirty and spread disease

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks animals like to be together as much as possible.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It keeps them warm" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw a small hutch with ten rabbits; ask what happens to the droppings and the food.
misconceptions.feedback: Give each rabbit enough space. Crowding causes fights and disease.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks scratching and hair loss in a rabbit are normal.

example.question: A rabbit scratches a lot and has bare patches. What should be done?
example.correct_answer: Check for mites, separate it and ask an adult or vet for treatment

misconceptions.cause: The child does not know small animals get parasites.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing, rabbits do that" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a picture of mange on a rabbit's ear.
misconceptions.feedback: Scratching and bare patches mean mites. Separate the rabbit and get it treated.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Stores produce before it is dry.

example.correct_answer: In a clean closed container, off the floor

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "On the floor in an open sack" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves the drying produce out overnight.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Stores the produce while it is still soft and moist inside.

example.correct_answer: It is crisp and breaks easily

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It has been in the sun one day" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.

skills.name: Name the basic crochet stitches, the tool and the articles made
skills.mastery: The child says crocheting uses one crochet hook and yarn (not two needles), that the chain stitch is the base and begins every piece, that the slip stitch joins, that the single crochet is short and the double crochet taller, and names articles made (a doily, a table mat, a coaster, a small bag). Crocheting is practical. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 Agriculture and Nutrition introduced it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Telling stitches apart by how they look began with running and back stitch. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.name: Say how a crocheted article is made, from slip knot to fastening off
skills.mastery: Says how a crocheted article is made: hold the hook and yarn, make a slip knot, a chain of the needed length, turn and work rows of single or double crochet (with the turning chain), keep the tension even, fasten off and weave in the end; in the app the child picks the right step, order, tool or reason in new situations. The practical (making a household article with crochet stitches) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: The child names the stitches and the tool before making an article. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
The chain is measured to the size the mat or wiper needs. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.assessed_by: teacher marks the practical with the KICD rubric

misconceptions.error: Says crocheting uses two knitting needles.

example.question: What is used to crochet?
example.correct_answer: One crochet hook and yarn

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes crocheting and knitting.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Two knitting needles" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show the hook and two needles.
misconceptions.feedback: Crocheting uses one hook and yarn.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up which stitch comes first.

example.question: Which stitch is the base of a crocheted piece?
example.correct_answer: The chain stitch

misconceptions.cause: The child does not know the order.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Double crochet" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Start a piece with a chain.
misconceptions.feedback: The chain stitch begins every piece.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says single crochet is taller than double crochet.

example.question: Which stitch is taller?
example.correct_answer: Double crochet

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes the names.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Single crochet" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Crochet a row of each and compare.
misconceptions.feedback: Double crochet is taller than single crochet.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks crochet makes only clothes, not household articles.

example.question: Which household article can be crocheted?
example.correct_answer: A table mat, a cleaning rug or a surface wiper

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen crocheted clothes only.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only a sweater" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a crocheted mat and a kitchen wiper.
misconceptions.feedback: Crochet makes mats, rugs, wipers and bags for the home as well as clothes.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Forgets the turning chain at the end of a row, so the edges slope in.

example.question: Why is a turning chain made at the end of each row?
example.correct_answer: To lift the yarn to the height of the next row so the edges stay straight

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the chain as an extra stitch to skip.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is not needed" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a square with turning chains and one without; compare the edges.
misconceptions.feedback: Make a turning chain at each row end: one for single, three for double crochet.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Does not count the chain, so the mat comes out the wrong size or crooked.

example.question: Why count the stitches in the first chain?
example.correct_answer: The chain sets the width of the article; every row then has the same number

misconceptions.cause: The child crochets until it looks long enough.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is not needed" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare two wipers: one counted, one not; measure the widths of the rows.
misconceptions.feedback: Count the chain and the stitches in each row so the article is the right size and straight.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Pulls every stitch very tight to make the work strong.

example.question: What happens if crochet stitches are pulled too tight?
example.correct_answer: The hook cannot go in and the article curls

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks tight means strong, as with knots.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The work is stronger" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Try to push the hook into a very tight chain.
misconceptions.feedback: Keep the tension even and loose enough for the hook to go in.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Cuts the yarn at the end without pulling it through the last loop.

example.question: How is crochet finished?
example.wrong_answer: Cut the yarn and leave it
example.correct_answer: Cut, pull the end through the last loop and weave it in

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks cutting ends the work.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Cut the yarn and leave it" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pull a finished piece cut without fastening: it unravels.
misconceptions.feedback: Fasten off by pulling the end through the last loop, then weave it in.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: search and share information on the meaning of moist bed garden,
construct a moist bed (sunken or raised moist bed) using locally available materials,
establish and grow a crop of their choice to embrace the use of moist bed garden.
key_inquiry_questions: How can we construct a moist bed gardens to grow crops?
sub_strands.core_competences: Communication and collaboration: team work as learners share information on moist bed garden.
sub_strands.values: Respect: appreciation of diverse opinion as learners share information on moist bed garden.
sub_strands.pcis: Environmental conservation as learners use locally available materials to construct moist bed garden.
sub_strands.links: Learners relate skills used in construction of moist bed garden to craft skills learnt in Creative Arts.

outcomes.text: explain the meaning of moist bed garden
construct a moist bed garden for growing a selected crop
embrace the use of moist bed garden in growing crops

skills.name: Say what a moist bed garden is and how it is built
skills.mastery: The child says a moist bed garden is a sunken bed with layers of dry plant matter and manure under the topsoil and mulch on top, which holds water so that vegetables such as kale and spinach grow in dry times, puts the steps in order (choose a site near water, dig, add layers, add topsoil, plant, mulch, water), and does not say it is a raised bed. Building it is practical. The practical (constructing a moist bed garden and growing a crop) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say what a moist bed garden is
put the building steps in order
find the false step in a learner's plan

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 Agriculture and Nutrition introduced it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Sunken beds that hold moisture (Grade 6 1.2) are the base of a moist bed garden. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.assessed_by: teacher marks the practical with the KICD rubric

misconceptions.error: Says a moist bed garden is a raised bed.

example.question: What is a moist bed garden?
example.wrong_answer: A raised bed above the ground
example.correct_answer: A sunken bed that holds water

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes the two beds.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A raised bed above the ground" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Dig and water a sunken bed.
misconceptions.feedback: A moist bed garden is sunken with layers that hold water.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts the steps in the wrong order.

example.question: What comes first in building a moist bed garden?
example.correct_answer: Choose a site near water and dig

misconceptions.cause: The child jumps to planting.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Plant the seedlings" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Write the steps on cards.
misconceptions.feedback: Choose the site and dig first, then add layers, topsoil, plant, mulch and water.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the mulch.

example.question: What goes on top of a moist bed garden?
example.correct_answer: Mulch such as dry grass

misconceptions.cause: The child does not see water leaving the soil.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare a mulched and an unmulched bed.
misconceptions.feedback: Mulch on top keeps the water in.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Makes holes in the bottom of the polythene lining.

example.question: Where are the holes in a moist bed lining made?
example.wrong_answer: In the bottom, so water drains
example.correct_answer: Near the top only, so water collects below and too much can escape

misconceptions.cause: The child copies the drainage holes of a sack garden.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "In the bottom, so water drains" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Fill a lined tray with holes in the bottom and one with holes near the top; water both.
misconceptions.feedback: A moist bed keeps water at the bottom. Holes go near the top, not the bottom.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.
